summary: Specifies the SIP P-Profile-Key private header, used in 3GPP IMS to give registrars and proxies the key of the profile matching the destination of a request. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A tag that tells phone systems which stored customer information to use.

questions: what is the sip p-profile-key header
what is a wildcarded public service identity
what does the i-cscf do with p-profile-key
subtitle: A private SIP header that passes a profile lookup key between two proxies in 3GPP IMS so the user database only has to match a wildcard once.

tldr.problem: In 3GPP IMS, two proxies handling one request may each ask the user database for the same profile. When the address is covered by a wildcard, the database must search through its wildcard entries each time, which can be expensive or slow.
tldr.mechanism: The first proxy (I-CSCF) learns the matching Wildcarded Public Service Identity and inserts it in a P-Profile-Key header. The second proxy (S-CSCF) uses it as the lookup key and removes the header before routing on.
tldr.outcome: The header cuts repeated matching work and avoids storing every individual identity in the database. It is for trusted 3GPP IMS networks only and must not be used elsewhere.

today: RFC 5002 is an Informational RFC and is updated by RFC 8217. It limits the header to trusted 3GPP IMS networks.

sections.title: The Problem: Repeated Wildcard Matching
sections.content:
In the 3GPP IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS), a set of proxies handling a request may need to consult the same user database. They normally use the destination SIP URI of the request as the lookup key.

A Public Service Identity is a SIP URI that refers to a service instead of a user. A Wildcarded Public Service Identity is a set of such identities that match a regular expression and share one profile. When a query arrives for an identity with no profile of its own, the database must go through its wildcarded entries until one matches. The RFC says this can be computationally expensive, time consuming, or both, and it would be done twice if two proxies ask.
sections.plainLanguage: A big club has a rule like 'every room named chatroom-something uses the same rules'. Looking up which rule fits takes time, and nobody wants to do it twice.

sections.title: The Idea and Its Requirements
sections.content:
The first proxy gets the matching Wildcarded Public Service Identity from the user database and sends it, piggy-backed in the SIP message, to the second proxy. The second proxy can then query the database with the wildcard directly.

An alternative, storing every individual identity together with its matching wildcard, was rejected as undesirable because its scalability and manageability are considerably worse. The two requirements are to optimize response time for session establishment in 3GPP IMS and to keep the size and maintenance of the user database manageable.
sections.plainLanguage: The first helper tells the second helper which rule applies. That is quicker than writing down every single room name in advance.

sections.title: The P-Profile-Key Header
sections.content:
The P-Profile-Key header holds the key a proxy uses to look up a given profile. Its value is a name-addr or addr-spec, optionally followed by generic parameters. The format of Wildcarded Public Service Identities is defined by 3GPP, and they take the form of Extended Regular Expressions (ERE) from IEEE 1003.1-2004.

The RFC's example carries a wildcard that would match identities such as sip:chatroom-12@example.com and sip:chatroom-657@example.com.
sections.plainLanguage: The header is a tiny label that holds the pattern, like 'chatroom-anything'.

sections.title: Where It Is Meant to Be Used
sections.content:
As with other P-headers, the RFC documents a limited applicability. The header is intended for 3GPP IMS networks, where it carries the key of a service profile stored in the user database (the HSS) between two proxies, the I-CSCF and the S-CSCF. Both belong to the same administrative domain and share a frame of reference to the database.

The I-CSCF inserts the header into a SIP request and the S-CSCF removes it before routing the request further. On the general Internet there are typically not multiple trusting proxies querying the same user database, so the header does not seem useful there.
sections.plainLanguage: The note only makes sense inside one company where both helpers share the same filing cabinet, and the second helper throws it away when done.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The header is for environments where elements are trusted and attackers are not supposed to have access to the messages between them, for example through IPsec or physical protection of the network. It MUST NOT be used in environments without these properties.

It needs integrity protection: an attacker who changes it could make the network apply a different service than the request calls for. It also needs confidentiality, because reading it would reveal how services are structured in a domain.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone swapped the sticky note, you would get the wrong shelf. And the note shows how the library is organized, so it should stay private.

data.title: P-Profile-Key
data.code:
P-Profile-Key = "P-Profile-Key" HCOLON (name-addr / addr-spec)
                *( SEMI generic-param )

P-Profile-Key: <sip:chatroom-!.*!@example.com>
